title: Growth of Nationalism
tagline: The factors that created an all-India nationalism, the founding of the Congress, and the moderate and extremist strands.

overview.intro: Nationalism in India was assembled rather than inherited: it required a shared sense of grievance, the material means to communicate it, and an organisation capable of speaking for the country as a whole. This unit examines the factors that gave rise to Indian nationalism, the founding and early programme of the Indian National Congress, the differences between the moderate and extremist approaches, and the partition of Bengal and the swadeshi response that transformed the movement from a petitioning elite into a mass force.

learn.title: Factors leading to the rise of nationalism

blocks.text: Several developments in the second half of the nineteenth century made an all-India politics possible. English education created a class spread across the country that could argue in a common language and read the same newspapers, and it exposed that class to ideas of liberty, nationality and representative government at precisely when it was excluded from the highest offices. The railways, the telegraph and a unified postal system allowed leaders in Bombay, Calcutta and Madras to correspond within days. A growing press carried political argument to a reading public, and the rediscovery of India’s past through archaeology, translation and literature supplied a shared history.

blocks.caption: Factors behind the rise of nationalism
rows: A common language of political argument and access to European ideas of liberty
Public debate across regions and a shared political vocabulary
Movement of leaders, ideas and petitions at speed
Naoroji’s drain theory gave a measurable case against colonial rule
A sense of shared history and civilisation
High posts reserved for Europeans despite Indian qualifications

items: A shared grievance is necessary before a shared identity can be organised.
Communication infrastructure converts parallel resentments into one movement.
Economic arguments made the case quantifiable rather than merely sentimental.
Cultural revival supplied pride where the colonial order supplied deference.

learn.title: The founding and early programme of the Congress

blocks.text: The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885, its first session held in Bombay with seventy-two delegates, after earlier attempts such as the Indian National Association of Surendranath Banerjee. The early leadership included both Indians and retired British officials, and the Moderates who dominated it believed that reasoned petition would persuade a just administration to reform. Their demands were for a greater share of Indians in the legislative councils, the reduction of the home charges, the appointment of Indians to high posts, protection for Indian industry through tariff reform, and an end to the worst administrative violence.

The achievement of the Moderates should be judged by what was obtainable in their period: they created a national forum that met every year, trained a generation in political debate, supplied an economic critique that endured, and won some concrete concessions, including the expansion of council membership under the Councils Acts of 1892 and 1909. Their limit was equally clear: their base was the English-educated urban middle class, their methods excluded mass participation, and their loyalty to constitutional means made them slow to respond when the administration showed no willingness to go further.

blocks.caption: Moderate and extremist compared
rows: Petition, prayer, resolution, loyalty to the crown
Students, professionals and the urban public
Tilak, Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal

learn.title: The two strands and the Surat split

blocks.text: The Moderates held that Indians should first demonstrate competence in a small sphere of self-government before asking for more, and that criticism should be factual and moderate in tone. The Extremists replied that two decades of prayer had produced too little, that loyalty where it was not returned merely invited contempt, and that swaraj must be sought by mass methods and not by resolution alone. Bal Gangadhar Tilak’s defence of the assassinated officers of the 1897 Chapekar brothers case, his newspaper Kesari, and his imprisonment made him the symbol of the militant position.

The two wings came into open conflict at the Calcutta session of 1906 and finally split at Surat in 1907, where the Moderates used their majority to keep the Extremists from the Congress presidency. The split weakened both: the Congress lost its militant edge, the government prosecuted the Extremist leaders and closed their papers, and the constitutional reforms of 1909 satisfied neither side. Reunion came only at Lucknow in 1916, where the two wings reconciled and the Lucknow Pact agreed a joint scheme of council representation with the Muslim League.

items: The Moderates supplied the platform; the Extremists supplied the mass appeal.
The Surat split of 1907 was about methods and control of the organisation.
Government repression hit the Extremists after the split while conceding councils.
The Councils Act of 1909 introduced separate electorates, dividing rather than uniting.
Lucknow in 1916 reconciled the wings and produced a Congress–League agreement.

learn.title: The partition of Bengal and the swadeshi response

blocks.text: Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal in 1905 ostensibly on administrative grounds, dividing a province of some eighty million people, but the effect was to break the dominant position of Bengali nationalism by creating a new Muslim-majority province of Eastern Bengal and Assam. The response was immediate and nationwide: the day of the partition was observed as a day of mourning, Rabindranath Tagore led people to wear homespun cloth, and a programme of swadeshi, boycott, national education and national festivals was adopted. Foreign cloth was publicly burnt, students formed volunteer corps, and native industries such as textile mills and soap works expanded under the protection of the movement.

blocks.caption: The four elements of the swadeshi programme
rows: Use and manufacture of Indian goods in preference to foreign
Refusal to buy foreign cloth and, in its stronger form, of foreign titles and institutions
Schools and a national college teaching in the vernacular
Public occasions that created a political community

blocks.text: The movement demonstrated that politics could reach beyond the council chamber into the bazaar and the school, and it produced both industrial expansion and a new generation of leaders. It also revealed the limits of a movement without a mass social base: by 1908 the agitation had spent itself, and the government satisfied the Moderates with a further constitutional reform while the Extremists were prosecuted. Bengal was annulled in 1911, which showed that sustained pressure could force a reversal.

items.text: Public burning of foreign cloth in a Calcutta street in 1905.
items.note: Boycott made visible and collective, turning a private purchasing decision into a public act.

items.text: The establishment of the Bengal National College with Aurobindo Ghosh as principal.
items.note: National education attempted an alternative institution rather than reforming the existing one.

questions.answer: A division that weakened Bengali nationalism by creating a Muslim-majority province
questions.explanation: The effect was to break the dominance of the Bengali leadership, and it provoked the swadeshi movement as a response.

questions.prompt: The slogan swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it is associated with Bal Gangadhar __________ .
questions.explanation: Tilak was the leading extremist voice, whose newspaper Kesari and later imprisonment made him a symbol of the militant strand.

questions.prompt: The Congress and the Muslim League reconciled their differences over council representation at the __________ Pact of 1916.
questions.explanation: The Lucknow Pact both reunited the Moderates and Extremists and agreed a joint scheme of representation with the League.

questions.prompt: State four factors that led to the rise of Indian nationalism.
questions.answer: Four factors are: English education, which gave Indians access to ideas of liberty and a common language in which to argue; the growth of the press and the railways, which allowed political ideas and leaders to move across the country; the economic critique of colonial rule, particularly Naoroji’s drain theory, which made the case measurable; and the exclusion of Indians from high office despite their qualifications. The rediscovery of India’s past is also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each factor must be linked to the mechanism by which it built political consciousness.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the Moderates and the Extremists on three bases.
questions.answer: On method, the Moderates used petition, prayer and annual resolutions while the Extremists used swadeshi, boycott, national education and agitation. On goal, the Moderates sought reform within the British connection while the Extremists demanded swaraj as a birthright. On social base, the Moderates drew on English-educated professionals and the Extremists drew in students and the wider urban public. Their leaders also differed, with Naoroji and Gokhale on one side and Tilak, Lajpat Rai and Pal on the other.
questions.explanation: Three bases of comparison are required, each stated as a contrast rather than a description of one wing.

questions.prompt: Explain the swadeshi movement that followed the partition of Bengal, and assess its results.
questions.answer: When Curzon partitioned Bengal in 1905 the response took the form of a nationwide programme of swadeshi, boycott, national education and public political activity. Swadeshi meant the use and manufacture of Indian goods, and Indian textile and soap producers expanded as buyers turned away from foreign cloth. Boycott meant refusing foreign goods and, in its stronger form, refusing foreign titles and honours, and in practice cloth was publicly burnt as a symbolic act. National education led to the Bengal National College and schools that taught in the vernacular rather than through the prescribed system, and national festivals and volunteer corps created occasions for a shared political identity. The results were that politics was carried beyond the professional elite into the bazaar and the school, a generation of leaders was trained, and industry received a commercial stimulus. Its limits were that the movement could not be sustained past 1908, that it had little engagement with the peasantry and the lower castes, and that the government answered it with repression of the Extremists and conciliation of the Moderates. Bengal was nevertheless annulled in 1911, showing that sustained pressure could force a reversal.
questions.explanation: Full marks need all four elements with practice described, plus a balanced assessment of achievement and limit.

questions.prompt: Was the founding of the Indian National Congress in 1885 a turning point or merely a new debating society? Answer with evidence.
questions.answer: The case that it was a mere debating society rests on its early practice: the sessions were attended by a small number of English-educated professionals, the resolutions were addressed respectfully to the government, the methods excluded mass participation, and the demands were for incremental reform such as greater council representation and reduction of the home charges. The case that it was a turning point is stronger. The Congress created for the first time a forum that met annually and included delegates from every region, so that political demands could be formulated for the country as a whole rather than for one province. It supplied an enduring economic critique through Naoroji’s drain theory, which gave the movement an argument rather than only a sentiment. It trained a generation of leaders in organisation and debate, and its very existence meant that the administration now had to answer an Indian political body. The expansion of the councils in 1892 and the eventual attainment of the 1909 reforms show that the pressure produced results, while the later mass movements could not have operated without the platform the Congress had built. The judgement therefore has to be that its early methods were limited but its institutional effect was decisive, since the organisation it created was the vehicle through which every later demand was expressed.
questions.explanation: The answer earns marks for weighing both readings with specific evidence and reaching a reasoned judgement rather than asserting either extreme.
